newsitem.title: MOROCCO: World Bank offers emerging markets rules for success.
newsitem.headline: World Bank offers emerging markets rules for success.

text.p: One of the World Bank's top economists on Friday gave the recipe for joining the "club" of successful emerging markets - dominated by East Asian nations - attracting billions of dollars from foreign investors.

"Emerging markets now represent two percent of the portfolios of pension funds; two percent is not much but it represents $70 billion," said Luc de Wolf, principal economist for the bank's Middle East and North Africa division.
He told a capital markets and investment forum that pension fund assets had risen 150 percent in the five years to 1994 and ran into trillions of dollars.

Mutual funds also invested about two percent in emerging markets, meaning another $35 billion. Growth from both these sources would continue, he forecast, while official foreign capital flows stagnated, in part from "aid fatigue"
He pointed out that 12 countries took 95 percent of capital flows to emerging markets.

To join this group, dominated by Asian "Little Dragon" nations, countries had to know what investors wanted. Driven by competition they were seeking "high return and opportunities for risk diversification."
The World Bank expected East Asian countries to grow at an annual eight percent to the year 2000, while OECD nations would grow at only three percent.
Among essentials to attract investment, de Wulf said a sound macroeconomic system was a "mantra" for the World Bank.

"Soundness of a macroeconomic system enhances the profitability of investments. Hence if it is not sound, why would an investor look at a country where profitability is undermined by high inflation, high current account and fiscal deficits," de Wulf asked.
Reforms needed to enable private investors to make a profit and should have a "less xenophobic attitude to investment."
"Low labour costs are essential for many investors," he said, adding this did not necessarily mean low wages but more efficient use of labour.
"It is efficiency which counts ... a result of education and professional training. The importance that we give at the World Bank for emerging markets is education."
Low taxation was also important, said de Wulf, adding that Morocco's halving of taxation in five years was "a giveaway".
But more important was an "enabling environment".
"The ease with which an operation can be started, the ease of operating and the ease of closing an operation. Rules must be clear and be enforced," he said.
This environment was equally vital for domestic investors who provided three-fifths of investment in emerging markets.
And he added: "Large portfolio flows are not possible without a large capital market, a supply of domestic paper."
"For all foreign investors, it is always the same question: 'do you believe the bourse functions?'," he said.
